prompt: A single panoramic scientific illustration centers on a geometric bacteriophage, its icosahedral protein head packed with a tiny coiled genome, landing like a lunar module on one specific rod-shaped bacterium while ignoring neighboring bacterial species of different shapes and colors; the phage’s tail injects its genetic instructions as a glowing stream, after which the bacterium swells and ruptures, releasing a swarm of identical new phages. Human cells and tissues in the same frame remain completely untouched and healthy, emphasizing that the virus never infects people. In the surrounding laboratory-and-clinic setting, a computer screen displays an AI system assembling and rewriting those same minuscule genomes into novel sequences, while a physician administers the resulting custom phages to a patient whose infection has already shrugged off conventional antibiotic pills; a few surviving bacteria display mutated surface proteins that confer resistance, visually arguing why researchers must keep designing fresh phages rather than relying solely on those found in nature, and a discreet world map in the corner marks the countries already using this therapy.
